pages.text:
CODERED ’26 Challenge Brief: Customer Knowledge Graph for Hybrid
B2B Commerce

As of 27 October 2026
Challenge at a glance

Build a centralised customer knowledge graph that lets a hybrid online-plus-field-sales B2B
company in India know who its customers are, what they are working on, and whom to call
next.

Challenge         An Indian B2B e-commerce marketplace for robotics, industrial automation,
Partner           electronic components, drones and 3D printing, selling online and through a
                  field sales team. The company is not named in this brief.
Domain            Knowledge graphs, entity resolution, data engineering, applied AI, B2B sales
                  enablement
Users of the      Field sales, inside sales, marketing, leadership
product
Data              Open and public sources. Teams simulate the company’s internal data.
Format            About one month of remote build, two online evaluation rounds, then a 24-
                  hour on-campus sprint at BMSITM on 3 and 4 December 2026
What we           A working graph and the four sales workflows it powers (account brief,
want to see       territory query, lead discovery, next-need signals)
About the Challenge Partner

The partner is an India-based B2B marketplace with a large multi-brand catalogue
spanning robotics, industrial automation, electronic components, drones and 3D printing.
Its customers include manufacturers, system integrators, defence suppliers, universities,
research labs, startups and individual engineers.
Sales happen two ways. Most orders arrive online through the website, where a buyer
creates an account, browses, and checks out with a GST number and a shipping address. A
field sales team handles the larger and repeat business: it visits customers, scopes projects
and quotes against requirements.

Every order, web session and sales visit leaves a trail of data. Today that trail sits in
separate systems and in salespeople’s heads. The partner wants it connected.
Why this is hard in India

A B2B buyer in India is known only in fragments: a GSTIN on an invoice, a PIN code on a
shipping label, a personal Gmail address on a web account, and a company name spelled
three different ways across three orders. Nothing ties those fragments together.

In the US or Europe a company would buy that stitching from a data aggregator and get a
ready company profile with industry, size, location and contacts. India has no equivalent
with real depth on SMEs, integrators, labs and startups. The information exists, but it is
scattered across the GST portal, MCA company filings, Udyam registrations, customs and
import records, tender portals, company websites, job posts and news, each in its own
format and with its own quirks.
The internal side is just as fragmented. The order system knows what was bought and
where it was shipped. Web analytics knows what was browsed, from which device and IP.
The CRM, where one exists, knows what a salesperson typed after a meeting. None of these
share an identifier.
So a sales rep walks into a meeting knowing only the customer’s last order. Marketing
targets by city rather than by need. Leadership cannot answer a question as basic as “how
many pharma manufacturers in Hyderabad buy from us?” without a week of spreadsheet
work.
The problem statement

Design and build a customer knowledge graph: one connected model that resolves every
signal about a customer, internal and external, into entities and relationships, and exposes
it to a sales team through plain queries and ready-made briefs.
The company already holds four kinds of data for every customer:
  •     Order history: SKUs, HSN codes, quantities, values, invoice GSTIN, and billing and
        shipping addresses with PIN codes.
  •     Web behaviour: pages, categories, searches, carts, and time on site.
  •     Account details: company name, email domain, and phone.
  •     Session metadata: IP address, device, user agent, and mobile or desktop.
With effort, more is publicly available: GSTIN registration details (legal name, state,
registration type), MCA company master data (incorporation date, directors, registered
office), Udyam MSME registrations, import and export records, government tenders and
awards, patents, funding and hiring news, company websites and LinkedIn pages.
The graph must turn all of this into answers to questions a human could not answer from
the raw data. Six problems sit inside that:

  1.    Entity resolution: decide that “ABC Automation Pvt Ltd”, “abc automation”, a GSTIN,
        a Gmail account and a shipping PIN all refer to one company, and say how confident
        you are.
  2.    Enrichment from the internet: find and attach what open portals, scraped pages and
        third-party data services say about that company, and corroborate it across sources,
        because no single external source can be trusted on its own.
  3.    Graph modelling: a schema that connects accounts, people, locations, products,
        orders, sessions and external records, and survives new data types.

4.    Inference: derive what is not stated anywhere, such as industry, project activity,
        buying stage, or the product a customer will need next.
  5.    Access for non-technical users: a salesperson on a phone, before a meeting, must get
        an answer without writing a query.
  6.    Freshness and trust: facts change, sources go down, and every claim must be
        traceable to where and when it came from.
How teams solve these is open. Graph databases, relational models, vector search, rules,
classical ML and large language models are all acceptable, alone or combined. The company
defines the opportunity. The team defines the solution.
The graph resolves internal and public fragments into one account, corroborates them
across sources, scores them for confidence, and serves them back as the four things sales
asks for.
Who the users are

The primary user is a salesperson with ten minutes before a meeting and a phone in hand.
Everyone else is secondary.

                      What they need
User                  from the graph               A question they would ask
Field sales rep       A one-page brief             “What has this account bought in 12 months,
                      before a visit               what are they browsing now, and what projects
                                                   are they running?”
Inside sales /        A daily list of who to       “Which customers in this PIN code range have not
telecalling           call and why                 ordered in 90 days?”
Marketing             Segments built on            “Every drone-component buyer in Maharashtra
                      need, not geography          with a GST registration, by industry”
Leadership            Territory and                “Where are our top 100 automation customers
                      category planning            concentrated, and who nearby looks like them?”
What a solution must achieve

The final product must power all four workflows below from one graph, on a dataset messy
enough to prove the resolution works.
  1.    Account brief: given a company name, GSTIN, email domain or phone number,
        produce a brief a rep can read on a phone: who they are, where they are, what they
        buy, what they have been browsing, what the public record says they are working
        on, and what to pitch.
  2.    Territory and segment query: given a PIN code, city, district, industry or product
        category, return the matching customers ranked by value and recency, with enough
        context to plan a day of visits.

3.    Lead discovery: given the existing customer base, surface companies in the public
        record that look like good customers but have never ordered, with the evidence for
        why.
  4.    Next-need signals: for a customer, infer what they are likely to need next from their
        own history, from similar customers, and from external signals such as a new
        import, tender or hire.
Across all four, the product must:
  •     Resolve identities across inconsistent names, personal email addresses, multiple
        shipping addresses and shared IPs, and expose a confidence score for every merge.
  •     Carry provenance: every fact shows which sources support it and when each was
        last seen.
  •     Degrade gracefully: a missing or unreachable source lowers confidence rather than
        breaking the answer.
  •     Be usable by a non-technical salesperson without training. A natural-language
        interface is welcome but not required. A well-designed form or search is acceptable.
  •     Update incrementally as new orders, sessions and external records arrive, without a
        full rebuild.
Data you can work with

The partner provides no internal company data. Teams design and generate a synthetic
internal dataset that mirrors what the company holds, and it must be realistic in its mess:
company names typed three ways, personal Gmail addresses on business accounts, several
shipping PIN codes per customer, shared office IPs, and a GSTIN on some orders but not
others.

Internal source to
simulate                   Fields
Orders                     order id, date, SKUs, HSN codes, quantities, value, invoice GSTIN,
                           billing and shipping address with PIN code
Web sessions               account or anonymous id, pages, categories, searches, cart events,
                           timestamps
Accounts                   company name as typed, contact name, email, phone, GST number if
                           given
Session metadata           IP address, device type, user agent, mobile or desktop

Enrichment from the internet: allowed, and the hard part

Teams may use language models (LLMs and RLMs) and any enrichment source on the
internet: open government portals, scraping of public web pages, and third                   -party data
services that expose company information through APIs or exports. All are permitted
within each source’s terms of use, and data gathered for the challenge is used for the
demonstration only.

Treat everything that comes from outside as a signal, never as a fact. Third-party services
in India are incomplete and inconsistent. They publish no measure of their own accuracy,
and there is no benchmark to check them against. The same holds for a scraped page or a
model’s extraction from one.
The central quality problem of this challenge is therefore corroboration rather than
collection. A claim about a customer earns confidence when several independent sources
agree, loses it when they disagree, and is marked uncertain when only one weak source
makes it. The graph should record, for every fact, which sources said it, when, and how
much weight it carries. How the team computes and shows that weight is its own design
decision. That the weight exists and can be defended is required.

Open starting point                                                What it can tell you
GST portal (GSTIN search)                                          Legal name, trade name, state,
                                                                   registration type and status
MCA company master data                                            Incorporation date, registered office,
                                                                   directors, company status
Udyam registration                                                 MSME classification and activity
Import and export records (customs and DGFT data,                  What a company imports, from
directly or through services that index it)                        where, how often
Tender portals (GeM, CPPP, state portals)                          Government projects bid for and
                                                                   awarded
Patent office filings                                              Technology areas a company is
                                                                   developing
Company websites, LinkedIn pages, job posts, news                  Products, projects, hiring, funding
India Post PIN directory, OpenStreetMap                            PIN code to locality, city and district
CBIC HSN master                                                    Product classification behind every
                                                                   order line
Third-party company data APIs                                      Aggregated profiles, usable as one
                                                                   signal among several

These are starting points, not requirements. A team that finds a better source and shows
why it can be trusted is doing exactly what the challenge asks.
Scope, constraints and compliance

The challenge is the graph and the four workflows on top of it. It is not a CRM, not a
storefront recommender, and not a scraper of individuals.

In scope                                                          Out of scope
Resolving companies, contacts, locations and                      Replacing the company’s CRM or
products into one graph                                           order system
Enriching accounts from open and third-party                      Product recommendations on the
sources, with corroboration and provenance                        public website

In scope                                                           Out of scope
Inferring industry, project activity and likely next               Building a general-purpose company
need, with evidence                                                database for India
Query and brief interfaces for sales, marketing and                Profiling individuals from personal
leadership                                                         social media accounts

Personal data. Contact names, email addresses, phone numbers, IP addresses and device
identifiers are personal data under India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.
Collect only what the workflow needs, keep it for a stated purpose, and show that a
person’s data can be found and deleted on request. Business identifiers such as a GSTIN, a
registered office or a company’s import record are not personal data, but the design should
still show restraint about how they are combined with data about individuals.

Deployability. The partner will run this on its own infrastructure. The architecture must
be deployable on private servers or a private cloud, with open-source components
preferred. Any hosted service, including a hosted language model, must be optional and
swappable. The product cannot depend on sending customer data to a third party to
function.
Freshness. Sources change and go down. The design must separate what was observed
from when it was observed, and must not present a two-year-old record as current fact.
Demonstration and evaluation

Each stage of CODERED ’26 asks for a little more of the product, and the on-campus sprint
asks for all of it.

Stage                       What we want to see
Online round 1: PPT         The graph model, the sources chosen and why, the corroboration
and video                   approach, and one workflow working end to end on the team’s
                            synthetic data
Online round 2:             A live query: give the panel a company name or a PIN code and show
pitch                       the answer, with its sources and confidence
On-campus sprint:           All four workflows on a dataset with deliberate conflicts, plus a clear
build and evaluate          account of what the system got wrong and how it knows

Evaluators will weigh, in roughly this order:
  1.    Resolution quality: how well fragments are merged, measured on a labelled messy
        set the team builds, with the false-merge rate reported alongside the match rate.
  2.    Corroboration and provenance: whether every external fact carries its sources and a
        defensible confidence, and whether disagreement between sources is visible rather
        than hidden.
  3.    Usefulness to a salesperson: whether the brief and the query results change what a
        rep would do in the meeting.
  4.    Query experience: speed, clarity and how little the user has to know to ask.

5.    Data handling: compliance with the personal-data and deployability constraints
        above.
  6.    Path to production: what it would take to connect real systems and keep the graph
        current.
What would impress:
  •     A measured match rate and false-merge rate on a hard labelled set.
  •     An explanation attached to every inferred fact.
  •     A brief that fits on one phone screen.
  •     Correct handling of Indian naming quirks such as “Pvt Ltd” versus “Private Limited”,
        transliterated names and abbreviations.
  •     PIN-to-district reasoning that survives a wrong digit.
  •     A system that says “unknown” when the evidence is thin instead of guessing.
What comes next

The Challenge Partner will consider standout team members for internships.
In line with CODERED’s student ownership principle, participation does not transfer
ownership or commercial rights over the team’s work to the partner. Any licensing,
collaboration or commercial engagement after the event is a separate discussion and
agreement between the partner and the team.
Questions about this brief during the challenge go to E-Cell BMSITM at ecell@bmsit.in.
